newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus lodges protests over Greek Cypriot killing.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus lodges protests over Greek Cypriot killing.

text.p: Cyprus lodged protests with members of the U.N. Security Council on Monday over the killing of a Greek Cypriot civilian by Turkish Cypriot forces after he strayed into the Turkish-held areas of the divided island.

Cypriot Foreign Minister Alecos Michaelides, who summoned ambassadors of the five permanent members of the Security Council, said he appealed to the five to "convey to Turkey that it is not possible to tolerate such acts".
"A man was murdered because he crossed 40 or 50 metres into the occupied areas without posing any threat to the Turkish troops," Michaelides told reporters.
"The political message (from the other side) is that instructions have been given to troops to execute in cold blood anyone crossing the buffer zone to the occupied areas," he said.
Michaelides said this was to "discourage all those wishing for a solution to the Cyprus problem".
The killing of Petros Kakouli, 58, raised to five -- four Greek Cypriots and one Turkish Cypriot -- the number of people killed along the buffer zone since June.

The island has been divided since Turkey invaded in 1974 after a Greek-engineered coup on the island. A Turkish Cypriot breakaway state in the north, recognised only by Ankara, was established in 1983.
Mediation attempts under United Nations auspices to reunite the island as a bicommunal bizonal federation have failed to breach the 22-year-old stalemate.
In Ankara Turkish foreign ministry spokesman Omer Akbel accused the Greek Cypriot side on the island of having "opted for a policy of tension rather than negotiations on the island".
"They have encouraged and supported such actions aiming at increasing the tension in the island," Akbel said.

He said the Greek Cypriot side refused an appeal of the U.N. secretary general to issue a joint statement for the leaders of the two sides to meet, a proposal for a military dialogue between the two sides and the suspension of Turkish and Greek airforce flights over the island.
The Cypriot government has proposed demilitarisation of the island and the deployment of a multi-national force.

It rejected any meeting with Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash until "common ground" was found on basic aspects of the Cyprus problem relating to issues of sovereignty, territory, the island's bid to join the European Union and security issues.
Earlier Britain's special envoy on the Cyprus problem Sir David Hannay condemned the killing.

"Anything that can be done to make incidents like that less likely to happen would be thoroughly worthwhile," said Hannay, who arrived in Cyprus on Sunday night to continue efforts to end the 22-year-old division of the island.
Turkish Cypriot officials said the man had crossed 200 metres (yards) into the self-proclaimed Turkish Cypriot state and ignored warnings to stop.
The man's son-in-law, who said he witnessed the shooting, said Turkish forces shot and killed Kakouli after he surrendered to them. He said they were in the area collecting snails at the time.
Kakouli's body was due to be handed over to the Cypriot authorities later on Monday.
